data.chapter: Medicine and Public Health Through Time
data.sourcePassage:
Ancient Greek medicine was important because some thinkers argued that illness had natural causes. Hippocrates encouraged doctors to observe patients carefully, record symptoms and look for natural explanations. This moved some medical thinking away from blaming illness only on gods or spirits.

The four humours theory became very influential. It claimed the body contained four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Health was believed to depend on keeping these humours balanced. Treatments such as bloodletting, purging and herbal remedies were based on restoring this balance. Galen, a Greek doctor working in the Roman Empire, built on earlier ideas. His writings became extremely respected in medieval Europe. For many centuries, doctors followed Galen because his work seemed logical and was supported by universities and religious authorities.

Medieval Islamic medicine was a major part of world medical history. From the 700s onwards, scholars in the Islamic world translated medical texts from Greek, Roman, Persian, Indian and other traditions. Important centres of learning included Baghdad, Damascus, Cairo and Cordoba. Scholars did not simply copy older knowledge — many discussed, questioned and developed it. Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, wrote works later used in European universities. Al-Razi, known as Rhazes, wrote about diseases including smallpox and measles.

Hospitals in parts of the Islamic world provided care, teaching and sometimes separate wards for different illnesses. Knowledge travelled through trade, conquest, translation and contact between cultures. In medieval Spain and Sicily, Arabic medical texts were translated into Latin, helping European scholars access ancient and Islamic knowledge. This challenges a simple Europe-only story of medical progress: British and European medicine were shaped by wider-world knowledge.

questions.question: What were the four humours according to ancient Greek medical theory?
options: Fire, water, earth and air
Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile
Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and iron
Pain, fever, swelling and infection
questions.modelAnswer: Blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile.

questions.question: Who was Ibn Sina (Avicenna)?
options: A medieval English physician who worked in London
An Islamic scholar whose medical works were later used in European universities
A Roman doctor who developed the four humours theory
A surgeon who introduced antiseptic methods
questions.modelAnswer: An Islamic scholar whose medical works were later used in European universities.

questions.question: Why did Islamic scholars' medical knowledge reach medieval European doctors?
options: European doctors travelled to Baghdad to study
Arabic medical texts were translated into Latin in places such as Spain and Sicily
Islamic doctors moved to European universities
European monasteries independently developed the same knowledge
questions.modelAnswer: Arabic medical texts were translated into Latin in medieval Spain and Sicily, allowing European scholars to access Islamic and ancient knowledge.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the idea that medical progress was mainly European?
options: The passage confirms that Europe led all major medical advances
The passage shows that medical progress depended on knowledge from multiple cultures and global communication
The passage argues that Islamic medicine was inferior to Greek medicine
The passage suggests that ancient Greek ideas were never challenged or improved
questions.modelAnswer: The passage challenges a Europe-only story by showing that Greek, Islamic and other traditions all contributed to medical knowledge, which spread through translation, trade and contact across cultures.

data.chapter: Medicine and Public Health Through Time
data.sourcePassage:
The Renaissance brought renewed interest in observation and the human body. Andreas Vesalius published detailed illustrations of human anatomy in 1543 after studying bodies through dissection. He showed that some of Galen's ideas were wrong because Galen had relied partly on animal dissections. Vesalius mattered not just for his corrections, but because he showed the importance of direct observation over simply trusting old authorities.

William Harvey, an English physician, published his explanation of the circulation of blood in 1628. He argued that the heart acted as a pump and that blood circulated around the body. These developments did not immediately cure disease, but they changed methods: observation, experiment, dissection and printed books became more important in medicine.

Edward Jenner investigated why people who had caught cowpox seemed protected from smallpox. In 1796 he tested this idea and his work helped develop vaccination against smallpox. Vaccination was different from older inoculation methods because it was safer. However, vaccination faced opposition from people who feared it was unsafe, unnatural or against religion. Ideas about inoculation had also travelled from other parts of the world, including Asia and the Ottoman Empire, showing that medical change often depended on global knowledge.

Louis Pasteur showed that microbes caused fermentation and could spoil liquids. Robert Koch identified specific bacteria that caused specific diseases, including tuberculosis and cholera. Their work established germ theory — the idea that microorganisms cause disease. Germ theory transformed medicine by improving understanding of how diseases spread, supporting cleaner surgery and encouraging vaccination research. However, scientific discoveries needed government action and public funding to become widely useful.

data.chapter: Medicine and Public Health Through Time
data.section: Public Health Reform and the NHS
data.sourcePassage:
The nineteenth century brought rapid urbanisation in Britain. Towns and cities grew quickly as people moved for factory work. Many working-class areas had overcrowded housing, polluted water and poor drainage. These conditions helped diseases spread.

Cholera was one of the most feared diseases of the period. Many people believed it was spread by miasma — bad or poisonous air. John Snow investigated a cholera outbreak in Soho, London, in 1854. He mapped deaths and noticed that many victims used water from the Broad Street pump. When the pump handle was removed, the outbreak declined. Snow's work was important because it used careful evidence and mapping to link disease to contaminated water, not bad air.

Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report argued that poor sanitation caused disease and that improving drainage and water supplies would save lives. Although Chadwick believed in miasma, his practical solutions often improved public health because clean water and sewers reduced waterborne disease. The Great Stink of 1858 — when hot weather made the polluted Thames smell terrible near Parliament — helped push politicians to support Joseph Bazalgette's major sewer system for London.

Joseph Lister applied germ theory to surgery in the 1860s. He used carbolic acid to clean wounds and instruments, reducing infection rates. His antiseptic methods connected scientific theory with practical hospital change.

Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould called Penicillium killed bacteria in a laboratory dish. Penicillin was developed as a usable medicine in the 1940s and mass-produced during and after the Second World War, transforming treatment of bacterial infections. The National Health Service began in Britain in 1948, providing healthcare free at the point of use and reducing the barrier of direct payment for millions of patients.

questions.question: What did John Snow discover about the 1854 cholera outbreak in Soho?
options: Cholera was spread by bad air from the River Thames
Cholera was spread by rats carrying the disease
Many victims used water from the contaminated Broad Street pump
Cholera was caused by overcrowding in workhouses
questions.modelAnswer: Many victims used water from the Broad Street pump, linking cholera to contaminated water.

questions.question: What was the Great Stink of 1858 and why did it matter?
options: A factory explosion that polluted London's air and caused protests
The bad smell from the polluted Thames that helped push Parliament to support sewer improvements
A cholera epidemic that killed thousands in London
A government report on poor housing conditions
questions.modelAnswer: The Great Stink was when the polluted River Thames smelled terrible near Parliament in hot weather. It helped push politicians to support Bazalgette's major sewer system for London.

questions.question: What was significant about Joseph Lister's work in surgery?
options: He invented the first anaesthetic for surgery
He used carbolic acid to reduce infection by applying germ theory to surgery
He mapped cholera deaths to find the source of infection
He developed the first antibiotic medicine
questions.modelAnswer: Lister used carbolic acid to clean wounds and instruments, reducing infection rates. His antiseptic methods applied germ theory directly to surgical practice.

questions.question: The passage says Chadwick believed in miasma but his solutions still improved public health. What does this suggest about the relationship between correct theory and useful action?
options: Only correct scientific theories can lead to health improvements
A wrong theory can sometimes lead to useful practical measures if those measures happen to address the real cause
Miasma theory was actually correct and miasma did spread disease
Chadwick's solutions had no effect on public health
questions.modelAnswer: The passage suggests that even a wrong theory (miasma) could lead to useful practical solutions (clean water, sewers) if those solutions happened to address the real cause of disease (contaminated water).
